summary: Provides a framework and requirements for operations, administration and maintenance (OAM) of Layer 2 VPN services, pseudowires and packet switched network tunnels. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies that rent private network links need ways to check the links are working. This lists what checking tools they need.

questions: what is a maintenance end point
subtitle: How to maintain, monitor, and troubleshoot Layer 2 virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: Layer 2 VPN services must be monitored and maintained across multiple service providers and network domains. Without a clear OAM framework, operators lack a standardized way to detect faults, measure performance, and isolate problems across these complex services.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a hierarchical OAM framework based on IEEE and ITU standards, organizing monitoring into domains with maintenance endpoints and intermediate points. It specifies requirements for fault detection, performance measurement, and cross-domain coordination.
tldr.outcome: The framework enables operators to monitor VPLS and VPWS services independently of the underlying transport while supporting multiple administrative domains.

today: RFC 6136 is an Informational RFC providing framework guidance for L2VPN OAM. It has not been obsoleted and continues to serve as a reference for OAM deployment in multi-domain VPN environments.

sections.title: What OAM Does for Virtual Networks
sections.content:
Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) covers five functional areas known as FCAPS: Fault Management, Configuration Management, Accounting Management, Performance Management, and Security Management. This document focuses on the first two: Fault Management and Performance Management.

Fault Management detects problems (hard failures like broken links or soft failures like software bugs), verifies them, isolates them to a specific device or link, notifies other systems, and recovers by switching to alternate paths. Performance Management measures metrics like frame loss, delay, and availability to verify that the service meets its objectives.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks need two jobs: spotting and fixing problems, and checking if everything runs fast and smooth. This document describes how to do both.

sections.title: Layering, Domains, and Maintenance Points
sections.content:
L2VPN services operate across multiple layers: the service layer (VPLS, VPWS) and network layers (MPLS/IP networks). Each layer is responsible for its own OAM. The framework organizes these layers into OAM domains—regions where OAM messages can operate unobstructed. An OAM domain may contain a customer (CE), a service provider (PE), or a network operator.

Maintenance End Points (MEPs) originate and terminate OAM messages at domain edges. Maintenance Intermediate Points (MIPs) sit between MEPs and relay OAM messages but never originate them. A Maintenance Entity (ME) is a point-to-point monitored association between a pair of MEPs.

OAM domains can be hierarchical (a lower-level MEP may correspond to a MIP in a higher-level domain) or adjacent (independent of each other). Filtering at domain boundaries prevents OAM messages from leaking between domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of checking stations along a mail route. A station at the end opens and closes mail bags. A station in the middle just passes them along. Different postal services guard their own sections.

sections.title: VPLS and VPWS OAM Frameworks
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) emulates a bridged LAN for a set of customer sites. VPLS OAM must cover the end-to-end service from customer edge to customer edge, including the bridge module, VPLS forwarder, and associated pseudowires (PWs). The framework defines OAM domains at the customer level (between CEs), the service provider level (between edge PEs), and the network operator level (between core PEs).

Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) offers a point-to-point service combining attachment circuits and a single PW between two PEs. VPWS OAM supports both end-to-end monitoring and segment monitoring to isolate faults. It accommodates different management models: one where the customer manages CEs and monitors end-to-end service, and another where the service provider manages both CEs and PEs.

In both services, MEPs and MIPs are identified using native addressing schemes (Ethernet MAC addresses for VPLS, native addressing for VPWS) and must be unique within their service instance and OAM domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A VPLS is like a virtual office with desks in multiple cities, all looking like one room. VPWS is like a dedicated phone line between two offices. Each needs different ways to check if it is working.

sections.title: What OAM Solutions Must Provide
sections.content:
VPLS OAM must support discovery (finding other devices in the same VPLS instance), connectivity fault management (detecting, verifying, localizing and notifying about faults), and performance measurement (frame loss, delay, delay variation, and availability). Fault notifications must propagate across layers so that client-layer alarms can be suppressed when server-layer faults occur.

OAM frames must follow the same data path as service frames to ensure accurate measurement. The solution must scale to support OAM for each VPLS instance and must be extensible for future enhancements. Critically, OAM frames must be prevented from leaking outside their domain while transparently passing higher-level OAM frames.

VPLS OAM must be independent of underlying transport technologies (MPLS, IP, Ethernet, ATM) and independent of applications carried by the VPLS. VPWS adds additional requirements for prioritization and the ability to handle heterogeneous attachment circuits and pseudowires.
sections.plainLanguage: The checklist: Can you find all the desks? Can you spot broken connections? Can you measure delay? Can you stop duplicate alarms? And it must not let messages leak where they should not go.

sections.title: Putting It Together
sections.content:
The document describes operational scenarios for VPLS OAM that illustrate how these components work together. For example, when checking end-to-end service integrity in a hierarchical VPLS spanning multiple service providers and operators, the framework supports both per-service OAM and segment OAM. This allows detection of faults at any level—customer access, service provider core, or operator networks—and isolation of the fault to a specific segment.

The framework accommodates different deployment models: VPLS with MPLS access, VPLS with Ethernet QinQ access, and VPLS as pure LAN emulation over MPLS. Each model may impose specific requirements on the PW OAM and PSN OAM layers below the service layer.
sections.plainLanguage: In a real network, multiple companies manage pieces of the route. The framework lets each company check its part and tell the others when something is broken.
